readerTitle: The costs and benefits that never show up on your bill
caseNote: 가상 사례 (할인 식료품점, 택배 물류센터, 오픈소스 도구) + 실제 연구 (쇼핑몰 앵커 매장 임대료)
insight: 거래 밖으로 새어 나가는 비용과 이익은 사라지지 않는다. 결국 규제, 평판, 협상, 가격의 형태로 사업에 되돌아오므로 미리 계산에 넣어야 한다.
misconception: 내 장부에 없고 법을 어기지 않았다면 내 비용이 아니다. 내가 남에게 주는 이익은 언젠가 저절로 보상받는다.

sources.text: Pashigian, B. P. & Gould, E. D. (1998). Internalizing Externalities: The Pricing of Space in Shopping Malls. Journal of Law and Economics, 41(1).
외부효과의 표준 경제학 개념 (Pigou, A. C. (1920). The Economics of Welfare)
식료품점, 물류센터, 오픈소스 도구 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Pashigian & Gould(1998)의 핵심 결론(앵커 매장이 일반 매장보다 제곱피트당 훨씬 낮은 임대료를 낸다)을 원문으로 다시 확인하세요. 구체적인 할인 폭 수치는 카드에 넣지 않았습니다.
Pigou(1920)를 외부효과 개념의 대표 출처로 적었습니다. 카드 본문에는 연도와 이름만 언급하므로 서지 정보를 확인하세요.
모든 가상 사례에는 수치를 쓰지 않았습니다. 물류센터, 식료품점, 오픈소스 사례는 illustrative 라벨이 붙어 있는지 확인하세요.

cards.title: The costs and benefits that never show up on your bill
body: Two businesses share one road. A busy discount grocery fills the street with shoppers, and many drop into the pharmacy next door. The grocery earns nothing from that.
Down the road, a parcel depot runs trucks at 5 a.m. Neighbors lose sleep and the road wears out. The depot pays nothing for that.
Neither number appears in either company's accounts. Both are real.

image.label: A grocery and a parcel depot on the same street
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 한 길 위에 왼쪽은 사람들로 붐비는 식료품점(옆 약국으로 손님이 흘러가는 화살표), 오른쪽은 새벽 트럭이 드나드는 물류센터(주변 집 창문에 불이 켜짐). 실제 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: The neighbors are complaining about your trucks.
body: You run the parcel depot. Trucks idle and beep while reversing from 5 a.m. Residents have started a petition. You break no law, and fixing it would cost money.
What do you do?

options.text: Nothing. It's legal, and it isn't your cost
options.feedback: You save money today. But the cost is real, and it tends to come back as stricter permits, curfews or a harder time hiring locally.

options.text: Reroute trucks, fit quieter alarms where allowed, and talk to residents
options.feedback: You pay a little now to shrink the harm itself. That's usually cheaper than a rule written for you by someone angry.

options.text: Offer residents gift vouchers to make up for the noise
options.feedback: It admits the cost exists, which helps. But the noise stays, and a payment can become an expected yearly bill.

cards.title: Both businesses price only what touches them.
body: The grocery sets prices from its own rent, staff and stock. The extra sales it creates for the pharmacy don't count, so it has no reason to stay open later or draw more crowds for its neighbor's sake.
The depot plans routes from its own fuel and wage costs. Lost sleep and road repairs don't count, so it runs more early trucks than it would if it paid for them.
One spills a benefit. One spills a cost. Same blind spot.

cards.title: Externalities
body: An **externality** is a cost or benefit of a deal that lands on people outside the deal. Economists have studied the idea since at least Arthur Pigou's work in 1920.
Negative externalities are costs pushed onto others: noise, pollution, traffic. Positive ones are gifts to others: foot traffic, a cleaner street, skills that staff carry to other firms.
Because prices leave them out, markets tend to produce **too much** of the first kind and too little of the second.

image.label: A deal between two people with arrows spilling out to bystanders
image.brief: 가운데 판매자와 구매자가 악수하는 장면. 그 바깥으로 빨간 화살표(소음, 교통)와 초록 화살표(손님 유입, 깨끗한 거리)가 주변 사람들에게 흘러나감. 단순한 인포그래픽 스타일.

cards.title: Shopping malls put a price on the spillover.
body: Big department stores in malls draw shoppers who then walk past every small shop. A 1998 study by Pashigian and Gould found that mall owners charge these **anchor stores** much lower rent per square foot than smaller tenants.
The owner is doing what the street can't. It sees the benefit the anchor creates for others, and pays for it through rent.
Economists call this *internalizing* an externality: turning a spillover into something someone pays or gets paid for.

image.label: Mall floor plan with a large anchor store and small shops
image.brief: 쇼핑몰 평면도. 양 끝에 큰 앵커 매장, 가운데 작은 매장들. 앵커에서 나온 사람들이 작은 매장으로 걸어가는 점선. 앵커 위에 "Lower rent", 작은 매장 위에 "Higher rent" 라벨. 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: Spillovers rarely stay outside for good.
body: Costs you push out often come back. Towns add delivery curfews, fees and permits. Customers and staff remember who was a bad neighbor.
Benefits you give away can be captured too, but only if you design for it. A shop that draws crowds can negotiate lower rent, partner with neighbors, or share the cost of street events.
When only a few parties are involved, a direct deal often works better than waiting for a rule.
cards.softwareNote: A platform where each new user makes it more useful for others creates a positive externality. Bulk emails, spam or heavy scraping push costs onto others, and inbox providers and websites respond by filtering or blocking.

cards.title: Not every side effect is worth fixing.
body: Spillovers are hard to measure. A complaint is not proof of a large cost, and spending heavily to remove a small one wastes money.
The reverse trap is just as common. Creating a benefit for others doesn't mean anyone will pay you for it. People happily use what's free.
Ask two questions: how big is it really, and who could pay or be paid for it?

cards.title: Now it's a free software tool.
body: Your software company maintains a free open-source tool. Thousands of companies use it, including rivals. It takes two engineers full-time. A board member wants to shut it down.
What do you do?

options.text: Shut it down. Rivals are getting value for free
options.feedback: You save two salaries, but lose what the tool gives you: hiring pull, reputation and an ecosystem built around your product.

options.text: Keep it free, and add ways to capture value: a paid hosted version or sponsorship from heavy users
options.feedback: The benefit keeps flowing to others, but some of it now flows back. The tool can pay for its own upkeep.

options.text: Keep it as is. It's good for the industry
options.feedback: The benefit to others is real. But with nothing coming back, the tool stays a cost that's easy to cut in the next tight budget.

cards.title: Count what spills over, not just what you pay.
body: Every business pushes some costs and benefits onto people outside its deals. Those spillovers tend to return as rules, reputation or deals, so plan for them.
**Try it today:** list one cost and one benefit your business creates for neighbors, customers' families or other firms. Who pays for each? Could a small change or a simple deal make it fairer?
